prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: [val] Code · CLI flags (language en).
Grid: 4 columns × 5 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Flag" · longest unbreakable word 106px · one-line width 204px
  col 2: header "Type" · longest unbreakable word 55px · one-line width 55px
  col 3: header "Default" · longest unbreakable word 114px · one-line width 114px
  col 4: header "Description" · longest unbreakable word 89px · one-line width 477px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 360px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 359px.
This table cannot fit without splitting words at 360px. You MAY choose a total wider than 359px (the reader then scrolls horizontally), or squeeze and accept splits — a design decision.
Rendering convention: the screenshot always shows the WHOLE table. Anything beyond the dashed box is not clipped; it is the part a reader reaches by scrolling sideways, so judge both what fits in the box at first sight and the cost of scrolling to the rest.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 360px (different strategies, not small variations).
An earlier design attempt for this table was rejected by independent reviewers. Their comments: another layout was rated acceptable: The flag identifiers stay intact and Type is easy to scan, but Default extends beyond the viewport and Description requires horizontal scrolling. The tall rows make the visible portion feel sparse. | another layout was rated acceptable: Type and Default fit at first sight, but several flags wrap and the Description column is beyond the viewport. The wrapped identifiers are less immediate to scan. | another layout was rated bad: All columns fit in the viewport, but the narrow Flag and Description columns break identifiers and ordinary words repeatedly. The resulting tall rows make comparison difficult. | another layout was rated poor: Flag identifiers wrap across multiple lines, while Description begins at the viewport edge and must be read by scrolling. The narrow description also produces tall rows. | your previous preferred design was rated acceptable: The first flag stays on one line, but longer flags wrap and the final default extends beyond the viewport. Description is offscreen, so understanding each flag requires scrolling. | another layout was rated good: The flag identifiers stay intact and the rows are relatively compact. The tradeoff is that part of Default and all of Description require horizontal scrolling.
another layout was rated poor: Everything fits in the viewport, but flag names, the address, the Description header and ordinary words split across lines. The narrow description makes rows excessively tall. | another layout was rated good: Type and nearly all of Default are visible initially, and flag names wrap into manageable pieces. The descriptions require horizontal scrolling. | another layout was rated acceptable: Flag names stay intact, but they consume much of the initial viewport; the default address and descriptions lie partly or entirely beyond it. The tall rows also leave substantial empty space in the visible columns. | your previous preferred design was rated acceptable: The flag column is narrower than in C, but longer flags wrap and the default address still extends beyond the viewport. Descriptions require scrolling. | another layout was rated good: Flag names stay intact and the visible rows are relatively compact. The default address is cut off at the viewport edge, and descriptions require scrolling. | another layout was rated acceptable: The default values fit and the start of Description is visible, but long flag names break over several lines and the description text requires scrol
Reply ONLY JSON: {"understanding":{"purpose":"","reading":"","groups":["columns that belong together and why"],"keep_intact":[""],"may_wrap":[""]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[int px per column, column 1 first],"idea":"one sentence"}]}

log.raw: {"understanding":{"purpose":"Document CLI flags, their value types, defaults, and effects.","reading":"Readers scan flag names to find an option, then compare its type and default before reading its description. On a phone, the initial viewport should make identification easy while keeping the cost of scrolling to explanations reasonable.","groups":["Flag and Description identify each option and explain what it does.","Type and Default describe the value accepted and the behavior when the flag is omitted."],"keep_intact":["Flag identifiers and their punctuation, especially long option names and placeholders.","Type names and default values, including the address and port."],"may_wrap":["Descriptions can wrap at word boundaries.","The short and long aliases in a Flag cell can wrap between aliases; existing row height from descriptions can absorb some wrapping."]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[225,76,135,300],"idea":"Keep every flag on one line and give descriptions ample room, favoring compact rows and easy scanning at the cost of horizontal scrolling."},{"name":"B","widths":[140,76,135,260],"idea":"Keep types and defaults visible initially while allowing flag names to wrap, with a generous description column reached by scrolling."},{"name":"C","widths":[127,76,135,180],"idea":"Bring the start of Description into the initial viewport and reduce total scroll distance, accepting more flag wrapping and taller descriptions."}]}
